Attempt the match of the possibly rewritten pattern against the first pattern-length characters of the base code, anchored at the start, and set the verdict to whether that match succeeded.
records.formula:
value = whole_digits_as_integer + decimal_digits_as_fraction
number_of_whole_digits = length_of_whole_part − 2
value_string = barcode[ num_start : num_end − 2 ]
base_code = barcode with barcode[ num_start : num_end − 2 ] replaced by that many zeros, unescaped

rounding.what: Nothing. The value is exactly the digits read with the decimal point inserted where the pattern says.
rounding.precision: As many decimal places as the pattern declares letters D.
rounding.step: Not applicable; no rounding is applied at any step.

result.name: the numeric value, the base code and the match verdict
result.unit_or_currency: a decimal number, a text and a verdict
result.stored_or_displayed: consumed by the parser, which turns them into a typed result

edge_cases.case: The pattern carries no brace group.
edge_cases.outcome: The value stays zero, the base code stays the barcode and only the plain match decides the verdict.

edge_cases.case: The whole part of the group is empty.
edge_cases.outcome: The whole digits are read as the single digit zero, so the value is a pure fraction.

edge_cases.case: The extracted whole digits are not all digits.
edge_cases.outcome: No value is computed and no rewriting takes place; the pattern is matched as it stands.

edge_cases.case: The barcode carries a brace, a backslash or a full stop.
edge_cases.outcome: The escaping neutralises it, and the four escapes are reversed in the same order when the base code is produced.

edge_cases.case: The pattern is shorter than the barcode.
edge_cases.outcome: Only the first pattern-length characters of the base code take part in the match, so a pattern matches a prefix rather than the whole barcode.

worked_examples.description: A weight-embedded label matched against a pattern with a two-and-three digit numeric field
worked_examples.narrative: The value string is the five characters the numeric field occupies. Two of them are whole digits, giving one, and three are decimals, giving zero point two five zero, so the value is one point two five. The base code has those five positions blanked with zeros, and the rewritten pattern matches it character for character.

records.name: Parsing a barcode against a classic nomenclature
records.purpose: Turns a scanned string into one typed result — a type, an encoding, a code, a base code and a value — by trying the nomenclature's rules in order.

operands.name: scanned string
operands.source: the scanner or the caller
operands.constraints: a string beginning with `urn:` is decoded as a uniform resource identifier instead

operands.name: rules of the nomenclature
operands.source: the nomenclature
operands.constraints: tried in ascending sequence then ascending identifier

operands.name: conversion policy of the nomenclature
operands.source: the nomenclature
operands.constraints: governs whether a scan may be re-encoded to satisfy a rule that demands the other scheme

preconditions.condition: The nomenclature is not a Global Standards One nomenclature.
preconditions.otherwise: The decomposition loop of the Global Standards One rules runs instead and returns an ordered list rather than a single result.

procedure: Decode the string as a uniform resource identifier and return that result when it begins with `urn:`.
Run the Global Standards One decomposition and return its list when the nomenclature is a Global Standards One nomenclature.
Otherwise initialise the result with an empty encoding, the type `error`, the code and the base code equal to the scanned string, and a value of zero.
For each rule in ascending sequence then ascending identifier, set the current barcode to the scanned string.
Prefix a zero to the current barcode when the rule demands `ean13`, the scanned string is a valid twelve-digit Universal Product Code and the conversion policy is `upc2ean` or `always`.

Otherwise drop the first character of the current barcode when the rule demands `upca`, the scanned string is a valid thirteen-digit European Article Number whose first character is a zero and the conversion policy is `ean2upc` or `always`.
Skip the rule when the scanned string — not the converted one — does not satisfy the rule's encoding.
Match the current barcode against the rule's pattern.

On a match with a rule whose type is `alias`, replace the scanned string by the rule's alias, set the result's code to that alias and continue with the next rule, because an alias is not a final answer.

On a match with any other type, set the result's encoding, type and value from the rule and the match, set the code to the current barcode, set the base code to the sanitised thirteen-digit form when the encoding is `ean13`, to the sanitised twelve-digit form when it is `upca` and to the match's base code unchanged otherwise, and return the result.
Return the initialised error result when no rule matched.
records.formula:
result.type = the type of the first matching non-alias rule, or `error`
result.value = the numeric value the pattern match produced, or 0
result.code = the current barcode of the matching rule, or the alias of the last alias rule, or the scan
result.base_code = sanitised_thirteen_digit( match_base_code )  when encoding = ean13
result.base_code = sanitised_twelve_digit( match_base_code )    when encoding = upca
result.base_code = match_base_code                              otherwise

rounding.what: Nothing; the value is carried exactly as the pattern match produced it.
rounding.precision: As many decimal places as the matching pattern declares.

result.name: typed parse result
result.unit_or_currency: an encoding, a type, a code, a base code and a decimal value
result.stored_or_displayed: consumed by the scanning screens, which look the base code up as a product, a lot or a package

edge_cases.case: No rule matches.
edge_cases.outcome: The result carries the type `error`, the scan as both code and base code, and a value of zero.

edge_cases.case: An alias rule matches and no later rule does.
edge_cases.outcome: The result's code is the alias and its type is `error`, so an unmatched scan that hit an alias reports the alias.

edge_cases.case: The conversion policy would re-encode the scan.
edge_cases.outcome: The conversion is prepared before the encoding check, but the check is applied to the original scan, so the conversion takes effect only for a rule with the `any` encoding or when the scan already satisfies the rule's encoding.

edge_cases.case: A chain of aliases is configured.
edge_cases.outcome: Each alias replaces the working barcode and the loop continues with the next rule, so a chain resolves forwards only and never restarts the list.

worked_examples.description: Parsing a weight-embedded grocery label
worked_examples.narrative: The scan passes the thirteen-digit check, the pattern extracts a weight of one point two five kilograms and blanks the weight field, and because the rule's encoding is the thirteen-digit European Article Number the base code is sanitised, its check digit becoming zero. The consuming domain looks up the product stored with that base code and records one point two five kilograms.

records.name: Dispatching a scanned uniform resource identifier
records.purpose: Recognises an electronic product code scanned as a uniform resource identifier and routes its data fields to the trade-item or the logistic-unit decoding, before any nomenclature rule is consulted.

operands.name: scanned string
operands.source: the scanner
operands.constraints: begins with `urn:`

operands.name: identifier kind and data
operands.source: the last two pieces of the string split on colons, each trimmed of whitespace
operands.constraints: the number of namespace segments before them does not matter

operands.name: data fields
operands.source: the data split on full stops
operands.constraints: their meaning depends on the identifier kind

preconditions.condition: The string begins with `urn:`.
preconditions.otherwise: It goes through ordinary rule-by-rule parsing.

procedure: Split the string on colons, take the last two pieces and trim the whitespace from each: the first is the identifier kind and the second is the data.
Split the data on full stops into a list of fields.
Run the trade-item decoding on all the fields when the kind is `lgtin` (lot-level Global Trade Item Number) or `sgtin` (serialised Global Trade Item Number).

Run the trade-item decoding on the fields after the first when the kind is `sgtin-96` (ninety-six-bit serialised trade item) or `sgtin-198` (one-hundred-ninety-eight-bit serialised trade item), the first field being a filter value.

Run the logistic-unit decoding on all the fields when the kind is `sscc` (Serial Shipping Container Code), and on the fields after the first when it is `sscc-96` (ninety-six-bit Serial Shipping Container Code).
Leave the string unchanged for any other kind, so that it goes through ordinary parsing.
records.formula:
identifier_kind = trimmed second-to-last piece of split( string , ":" )
data = trimmed last piece of split( string , ":" )
fields = split( data , "." )
fields_used = fields              for lgtin, sgtin and sscc
fields_used = fields after the first   for sgtin-96, sgtin-198 and sscc-96

rounding.what: Nothing; the operation is on text.

result.name: a list of typed results
result.unit_or_currency: records holding a type, a code and a value
result.stored_or_displayed: consumed by the scanning screens; every result carries the original uniform resource identifier as its base code and an empty encoding

edge_cases.case: The kind is not one of the six recognised ones.
edge_cases.outcome: The string is left as it is and goes through ordinary rule-by-rule parsing.

edge_cases.case: The scanner inserts whitespace around the final colon.
edge_cases.outcome: The trimming removes it, so the kind and the data are still recognised.

edge_cases.case: The string carries more namespace segments than usual.
edge_cases.outcome: Only the last two pieces are taken, so the extra segments are ignored.

worked_examples.description: Three kinds dispatched from their identifier
worked_examples.narrative: The first and third kinds use every field. The second drops its first field, the filter value of one, before the trade-item decoding sees the company prefix, the item reference and the serial.

records.name: Trade-item decoding of a uniform resource identifier
records.purpose: Rebuilds the product barcode and the tracking number carried by a serialised or lot-level trade item scanned as a uniform resource identifier.

operands.name: company prefix
operands.source: the first of the three fields used
operands.constraints: carried into the barcode unchanged

operands.name: item reference with its indicator digit in front
operands.source: the second of the three fields used
operands.constraints: its first character is the indicator digit and is moved to the front of the barcode

operands.name: tracking number
operands.source: the third of the three fields used
operands.constraints: used as it stands, both as the code and as the value of the lot result

preconditions.condition: Three fields are available after the dispatch has dropped any filter value.
preconditions.otherwise: The barcode cannot be rebuilt and the string goes through ordinary parsing.

procedure: Take the indicator digit, which is the first character of the item reference field.
Concatenate the indicator digit, the company prefix and the item reference without its indicator digit; that is the barcode without its check digit.
Compute the check digit of that string followed by the digit zero as a placeholder, and append it.
Produce a result of type `product` whose code and value are the completed barcode.
Produce a result of type `lot` whose code and value are the tracking number.
Give both results the original uniform resource identifier as their base code and an empty encoding.
records.formula:
product_barcode_without_check = indicator_digit + company_prefix + item_reference_without_indicator
product_barcode = product_barcode_without_check + check_digit( product_barcode_without_check followed by "0" )

rounding.what: Nothing; the operation is on digits.

records.name: The separator group of a Global Standards One nomenclature
records.purpose: Builds the optional trailing group every rule pattern is matched with, so that a variable-length value can be terminated while a fixed-length one still matches when nothing follows it.

operands.name: configured separator expression
operands.source: the nomenclature, when it configures one
operands.constraints: must be a valid expression; it must not match the beginning or the end of any rule's pattern

operands.name: the non-printing group-separator character
operands.source: the default when the nomenclature configures no expression
operands.constraints: used as an optional single character

preconditions.condition: The configured expression is valid.
preconditions.otherwise: The nomenclature is refused with the message reproduced in the business rules.

procedure: Wrap the configured separator expression in a non-capturing group and mark that group optional, when the nomenclature configures an expression.
Use the optional single non-printing group-separator character otherwise.
Append the group to every rule's pattern before matching, so that the separator is consumed together with the value it terminates.
Keep the group optional in every case, so that a fixed-length field not followed by a separator still matches.
records.formula:
separator_group = "(?:" + configured_separator_expression + ")?"     when the nomenclature configures one
separator_group = the optional single non-printing group-separator character   otherwise

rounding.what: Nothing; the result is a matching expression.

records.purpose: Removes the prefix some scanners put in front of the data, so that the decomposition loop begins at the first application identifier.

operands.constraints: compared in that order

Remove the first prefix that matches, and only that one.
Remove it once only, so a string carrying two prefixes keeps the second.
Hand the remainder to the decomposition loop.

remaining_string = scanned_string with its first matching prefix removed, once
recognised prefixes = `]C1` , `]e0` , `]d2` , `]Q3` , `]J1` , the non-printing group-separator character

records.name: Interpreting a matched pair whose content type is a measure
records.purpose: Turns the digits of a measure field into the number they stand for, placing the decimal point where the last digit of the matched application identifier says.

operands.name: matched application identifier
operands.source: the first capturing group of the match
operands.constraints: its last character is read as the decimal position when the rule's decimal-usage flag is set

operands.name: value string
operands.source: the second capturing group of the match
operands.constraints: must consist of digits only, or the interpretation fails loudly

operands.name: decimal-usage flag of the rule
operands.source: the barcode rule
operands.constraints: when cleared, the decimal position is zero and the value is a whole number

operands.name: associated unit of the rule
operands.source: the barcode rule
operands.constraints: carried with the value, for instance kilograms for a net weight rule

preconditions.condition: The last character of the matched application identifier is a digit when the decimal-usage flag is set.
preconditions.otherwise: The interpretation raises the message reproduced in the business rules, which names the rule and explains that a decimal rule must end its application identifier with a digit.

preconditions.condition: Every character of the value string is a digit.
preconditions.otherwise: The same message is raised, because the value cannot be read as a measure.

procedure: Set the decimal position to zero.
Read the decimal position from the last character of the matched application identifier when the rule's decimal-usage flag is set.
When the decimal position is greater than zero, split the value string that many digits from the right, insert a decimal point between the two parts and read the result as a decimal number.
When the decimal position is zero, read the whole value string as a whole number.
Raise the configuration message when any of the above fails.
records.formula:
decimal_position = last character of the matched application identifier, read as a digit, when the decimal-usage flag is set ; 0 otherwise
value = value_string_without_its_last_decimal_position_characters + "." + the_last_decimal_position_characters_of_value_string    when decimal_position > 0
value = value_string read as a whole number                                                                                      when decimal_position = 0

rounding.what: Nothing. The value is exactly the digits scanned with a decimal point inserted.
rounding.precision: As many decimal places as the decimal position says, before trailing zeros are dropped by the reading of the number.
rounding.step: Not applicable; a barcode-derived measure is never rounded.

result.name: measured value with its unit
result.unit_or_currency: the rule's associated unit of measure, for instance kilograms
result.stored_or_displayed: carried in the decomposition record and consumed by the scanning screen as a quantity

edge_cases.case: The decimal position is zero and the digits are all zeros.
edge_cases.outcome: The value is zero.

edge_cases.case: The split leaves trailing zeros in the fractional part.
edge_cases.outcome: They are read as part of the number, so one hundred and fifty-one point five zero zero zero reads as one hundred and fifty-one point five.

edge_cases.case: The application identifier ends in a character that is not a digit while the flag is set.
edge_cases.outcome: The configuration message is raised; this is a rule that is wrongly configured, not a bad scan.

edge_cases.case: The value string is longer than the decimal position.
edge_cases.outcome: The whole part is what remains on the left; when the value string is exactly as long as the decimal position the whole part is empty and reads as zero.

worked_examples.description: A net weight in kilograms with two decimals
worked_examples.narrative: The last character of the application identifier is two, so the six digits are split two from the right, giving twenty point zero four kilograms.

worked_examples.description: A rule with four decimals, scanned three times
worked_examples.narrative: The application identifier ends in four, so every value string is split four digits from the right: zero and zero zero zero zero, one and eight seven eight nine, one hundred and fifty-one and five zero zero zero.

worked_examples.description: The same three scans with the decimal-usage flag cleared
worked_examples.narrative: With the flag cleared the decimal position stays zero and each value string is read as a whole number.

records.name: Interpreting a matched pair whose content type is a numeric identifier
records.purpose: Validates the check digit of a trade item number or a container code found in a Global Standards One string, and rejects the rule quietly when it does not agree.

operands.name: value string
operands.source: the second capturing group of the match
operands.constraints: its last character is the check digit

operands.name: value string left-padded with zeros to eighteen characters
operands.source: derived from the value string
operands.constraints: padding makes the check computation independent of the field's declared length

preconditions.condition: The value string consists of digits.
preconditions.otherwise: The pattern would not have matched, because a numeric identifier rule declares a digit-only field.

procedure: Left-pad the value string with zeros until it is eighteen characters long.
Compute the check digit of the padded string.

Return nothing when that digit differs from the value string's last character, which tells the decomposition loop that this rule does not really apply and that the next one should be tried at the same position.
Otherwise take the value as the value string itself, kept as text and including its check digit.
records.formula:
padded = value_string left-padded with zeros to 18 characters
accept when check_digit( padded ) = last character of value_string
value = value_string, as text, check digit included

rounding.what: Nothing; the value stays text so that leading zeros are not lost.

result.name: numeric identifier value
result.stored_or_displayed: carried in the decomposition record and used to look a product or a package up

edge_cases.case: The check digit does not agree.
edge_cases.outcome: Nothing is returned and the loop tries the next rule at the same position; a wrong check digit is not an error.

edge_cases.case: The value string is shorter than eighteen characters.
edge_cases.outcome: The padding supplies the missing positions, so a fourteen-digit trade item number and an eighteen-digit container code use the same computation.

edge_cases.case: The value string is exactly eighteen characters.
edge_cases.outcome: No padding is added and the check digit is computed over the string itself.

edge_cases.case: The value carries leading zeros.
edge_cases.outcome: They are kept, because the value is text; the search preprocessing is what strips them when a stored barcode has to be found.

worked_examples.description: A fourteen-digit trade item number
worked_examples.narrative: Four zeros pad the fourteen digits to eighteen. The weighted total is one hundred and fifty-three, whose check digit is seven, and the value string ends in seven, so the record is produced with the value kept as text.

worked_examples.description: The same field with a mistyped last digit

expected_outputs.loop_behaviour: the next rule is tried at the same position

worked_examples.narrative: The digits disagree, so the rule returns nothing rather than failing; the decomposition continues with the following rule and abandons the whole string only when no rule applies.

records.name: Interpreting a matched pair whose content type is a date
records.purpose: Turns a six-digit date field into a calendar date, and rejects the rule quietly when the field is not six characters long.

operands.name: value string
operands.source: the second capturing group of the match
operands.constraints: must be exactly six characters

preconditions.condition: The value string is exactly six characters long.
preconditions.otherwise: Nothing is returned, the rule is treated as not applying and the loop tries the next rule at the same position.

procedure: Return nothing when the value string is not exactly six characters long.
Otherwise convert the six digits into a calendar date by the century-determination rule.
Raise the conversion message when the digits do not form a valid calendar date.
records.formula:
value = six_digit_date_conversion( value_string )   when length( value_string ) = 6
value = nothing                                     otherwise

rounding.what: Nothing; the result is a calendar date.

result.name: calendar date
result.stored_or_displayed: carried in the decomposition record and written onto a lot as its expiration date, its best-before date or its production date, according to the rule's type

edge_cases.case: The value string is five or seven characters.
edge_cases.outcome: Nothing is returned and the loop tries the next rule; no error is reported.

edge_cases.case: The day digits are two zeros.
edge_cases.outcome: The date is the last day of the month named, leap years accounted for.

edge_cases.case: The digits name an impossible day.
edge_cases.outcome: The conversion message is raised, quoting the underlying reading failure.

worked_examples.description: An expiration date field
worked_examples.narrative: The six digits are read as the year within its century, the month and the day; with a current year of two thousand and twenty-six the century is the twenty-first and the date is the thirty-first of December two thousand and twenty-six.

records.name: Interpreting a matched pair whose content type is an alphanumeric name
records.purpose: Carries a lot name, a serial number or any other text field through the decomposition unchanged, since such a field has no arithmetic of its own.

operands.name: value string
operands.source: the second capturing group of the match
operands.constraints: its accepted characters are fixed by the rule's pattern, which is what stops the greedy match at the separator

preconditions.condition: The pattern matched, which means the characters consumed are all in the class the rule declares.
preconditions.otherwise: The rule does not apply and the loop tries the next one.

procedure: Take the value string as the interpreted value, unchanged.
Produce the record with the rule, the rule's type, the application identifier, the value string and that value.
records.formula: value = value_string, unchanged

rounding.what: Nothing; the value is text.

result.name: alphanumeric value
result.stored_or_displayed: carried in the decomposition record and used as the name of a lot or a serial number

edge_cases.case: The value is empty because the field's minimum length is zero.
edge_cases.outcome: An empty value is produced; the rule still applies and the loop advances only if the match consumed the application identifier.

edge_cases.case: The field is variable-length and no separator follows it.
edge_cases.outcome: The greedy match consumes every following character its class accepts, which is the failure the separator exists to prevent.

edge_cases.case: The value carries digits only.
edge_cases.outcome: It is still text and is not unpadded here; the search preprocessing keeps a lot value out of the unpadding rewrite.

worked_examples.description: A lot number terminated by a separator
worked_examples.narrative: The class of the rule accepts the hyphen, the uppercase letters and the digits, and stops at the non-printing character, which the optional separator group then consumes.

worked_examples.description: The same lot number with the separator omitted from the label
worked_examples.narrative: Digits are in the accepted class, so the greedy match of up to twenty characters swallows the expiry field as well and the label loses its date. This is exactly the failure the separator prevents.

records.name: Converting a six-digit date
records.purpose: Decides which century a two-digit year belongs to and turns six digits into a calendar date, including the convention that two zero day digits mean the last day of the month.

operands.name: two-digit year within its century
operands.unit_or_currency: a whole number from zero to ninety-nine
operands.source: the first two digits of the field
operands.constraints: compared with the current year within its century

operands.name: two-digit month
operands.source: the middle two digits of the field
operands.constraints: must name a real month

operands.name: two-digit day
operands.source: the last two digits of the field
operands.constraints: two zeros mean that the day is not given

operands.name: current year and current century
operands.source: the current calendar year; the current century is that year divided by one hundred, discarding the remainder
operands.constraints: the conversion therefore depends on when it is run

preconditions.condition: The field is exactly six digits.
preconditions.otherwise: The date interpretation returns nothing before this conversion is reached.

procedure: Take the current calendar year and compute the current century as that year divided by one hundred, discarding the remainder.
Compute the difference as the two-digit year minus the current year modulo one hundred.

Choose the previous century when the difference is between fifty-one and ninety-nine inclusive, the next century when it is between minus ninety-nine and minus fifty inclusive, and the current century otherwise.
Form the year as the chosen century multiplied by one hundred plus the two-digit year.
Take the last day of that month in that year, leap years accounted for, when the day digits are two zeros.
Otherwise take that year, month and day, and raise the conversion message when the three do not form a valid calendar date.
records.formula:
current_century = floor_div( current_year , 100 )
difference = two_digit_year − ( current_year mod 100 )
century = current_century − 1    when 51 ≤ difference ≤ 99
century = current_century + 1    when −99 ≤ difference ≤ −50
century = current_century        otherwise
year = century × 100 + two_digit_year

rounding.what: Nothing is rounded; the century choice uses whole-number division and a remainder.
rounding.precision: Whole years, whole months, whole days.
rounding.method: Division discarding the remainder for the century.

result.name: calendar date
result.stored_or_displayed: carried in the decomposition record and written onto a lot

edge_cases.case: The day digits are two zeros in a February of a leap year.
edge_cases.outcome: The date is the twenty-ninth of February.

edge_cases.case: The two-digit year is more than fifty years in the future of the current one.
edge_cases.outcome: It is read as belonging to the previous century.

edge_cases.case: The two-digit year is more than fifty years in the past of the current one.
edge_cases.outcome: It is read as belonging to the next century.

edge_cases.case: The month and day do not form a real date.
edge_cases.outcome: The conversion message is raised, quoting the underlying reading failure inside the message.

edge_cases.case: The conversion is run in a different year.
edge_cases.outcome: The century chosen for the same six digits may differ, because the rule is relative to the current year.

worked_examples.description: Six conversions evaluated with a current year of two thousand and twenty-six
worked_examples.narrative: The second field has two zero day digits, so the date is the last day of March in two thousand and fifty-two. The third likewise gives the last day of February in a leap year, the twenty-ninth. The fourth names a fifty-first day and raises the conversion message. The fifth has a difference of fifty-four, which is in the range that chooses the previous century, so eighty reads as nineteen eighty; the sixth has a difference of forty-four, which stays in the current century, so seventy reads as twenty seventy.

records.name: The decomposition loop of a Global Standards One string
records.purpose: Breaks a scanned string into the ordered list of application identifier and value pairs it carries, or rejects it entirely when any part of it cannot be read.

operands.name: scanned string
operands.source: the scanner
operands.constraints: its symbology identifier is stripped first

operands.name: rules of the nomenclature whose encoding is `gs1-128`
operands.source: the Global Standards One nomenclature
operands.constraints: tried in ascending sequence then ascending identifier; only these rules participate

operands.name: separator group
operands.source: the nomenclature's configured expression or the default
operands.constraints: appended to each rule's pattern and always optional

preconditions.condition: Each candidate rule's pattern yields at least two capturing groups.
preconditions.otherwise: The rule cannot supply an application identifier and a value and is refused when it is configured.

preconditions.condition: The remaining string shrinks at every iteration.
preconditions.otherwise: The whole decomposition is abandoned, so that a rule matching the empty text cannot loop.

procedure: Build the separator group and strip the symbology identifier.
Start with an empty list of results and the whole remaining string.
For each rule whose encoding is `gs1-128`, in ascending sequence then identifier, attempt to match the rule's pattern followed by the separator group, anchored at the start of the remaining string.
Accept the first rule whose match succeeds, yields at least two capturing groups and whose interpretation returns a record.
Set the new remaining string to what follows the end of that match, separator included.
Abandon the whole decomposition and return nothing when no rule was found or when the remaining string did not shrink, because a partially decomposable string is not partially accepted.
Append the record to the results and repeat until the remaining string is empty.
Return the ordered list of records.
records.formula:
results = ordered list of records, one per matched pair
remaining_string( n + 1 ) = remaining_string( n ) minus the matched pattern and its separator
decomposition = nothing when any position matches no rule or when remaining_string does not shrink

rounding.what: Nothing at this level; each record's value is rounded, or not, by its own content type.

result.name: ordered list of decomposition records
result.unit_or_currency: records holding a rule, a type, an application identifier, a value string and an interpreted value
result.stored_or_displayed: consumed by the scanning screens, which resolve the product, the lot, the quantity and the dates in the order the records arrive

edge_cases.case: A rule matches but its interpretation returns nothing, for instance a numeric identifier with a wrong check digit or a date field of the wrong length.
edge_cases.outcome: The loop does not stop; it tries the next rule at the same position.

edge_cases.case: One position matches no rule at all.
edge_cases.outcome: The whole decomposition is abandoned and nothing is returned, however many pairs were already read.

edge_cases.case: Two application identifiers are prefixes of one another.
edge_cases.outcome: The rule sequence disambiguates them, because matching is anchored and the rules are tried in that order.

edge_cases.case: A variable-length field is followed by a fixed-length one with no separator between them.
edge_cases.outcome: The greedy match swallows the following field; placing the fixed-length field first avoids the need for a separator altogether.

worked_examples.description: A label carrying a trade item number, a lot and an expiry date

inputs.scanned_string: the group-separator character, then 019401909768545710LOT-A42, the group-separator character, then 17261231
